case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review the agency’s determination that alleged threats and mistreatment do not amount to “persecution” under the asylum statute using the highly deferential substantial-evidence standard (rather than more searching review).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the “persecution” element for asylum eligibility), together with the INA’s judicial-review framework requiring substantial-evidence review of agency factfinding (commonly applied under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the First Circuit gave too much deference to the Board of Immigration Appeals/Immigration Judge on the “persecution” question. In their view, whether a given set of threats and physical mistreatment rises to the legal threshold of “persecution” is not merely a raw factual finding; it is at least a mixed question (application of a legal standard to established facts) that warrants more meaningful appellate review to ensure uniformity and correct articulation of the persecution standard, particularly given systemic concerns about inconsistency in asylum adjudication.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues the First Circuit applied the correct standard: substantial-evidence review. It characterizes the issue as a fact-bound application within Congress’s chosen review scheme for immigration decisions, contending that ‘persecution’ determinations in this posture turn on the factfinder’s evaluation of the severity, frequency, and context of harm and threats. Under the INA, courts must uphold the agency unless the record compels the contrary conclusion, and petitioners’ objections are essentially disagreements with the agency’s weighing of the evidence rather than a legal error.
key_precedents: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024) (cited by the government in discussing standards of review and the law/fact distinction)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Jackson rightly press that Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson recognize some mixed questions as “questions of law” preserved by § 1252(a)(2)(D), and that courts must correct genuine legal misapplications. But that general preservation cannot be read to nullify Congress’s more specific instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that agency fact determinations are conclusive unless the record compels the contrary, especially where—per Justice Kagan’s reliance on Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai—the persecution call on a particular record is dominated by severity, frequency, and contextual judgment rather than a freestanding doctrinal construction. I would thus draw the narrow line Justice Sotomayor seeks for uniformity in a different way: de novo review for misstating the persecution standard, ignoring required factors, or adopting categorical rules, while treating the agency’s application of the correct standard to this record as reviewable only for substantial evidence. That reconciliation gives real work to both § 1252(a)(2)(D) and § 1252(b)(4)(B) and avoids inviting routine appellate reweighing in a high-volume docket.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson point is the strongest counter, but those cases interpret § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s general preservation of “questions of law” and do not erase Congress’s separate, specific instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that “administrative findings of fact” are conclusive unless the record compels a contrary result. As the Chief Justice explains, and as our cases like Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai reflect, the “persecution” determination on a given record is dominated by severity, frequency, and context—an evaluative, record-bound judgment that fits comfortably within the compelled-evidence framework rather than de novo appellate recalibration. Justice Sotomayor’s uniformity concern cannot justify recharacterizing that fact-laden application as pure “law” in a way that would drain § 1252(b)(4)(B) of meaning; de novo review remains available for genuine legal errors (wrong standard, categorical rules, ignored required factors). Because there is no showing here that the agency misstated the legal standard—as opposed to drawing a permissible, if contestable, line on this record—§ 1252(b)(4)(B) controls.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson point is the strongest push, and I agree those cases preserve review of bona fide “questions of law” notwithstanding jurisdiction-stripping. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1252(b)(4)(B) is a distinct, specific command that agency fact determinations are conclusive unless the record compels a contrary result, and our asylum precedents (Elias-Zacarias, Ming Dai, and Nasrallah) have consistently treated the persecution call on a particular record as an evaluative, severity-and-context judgment suited to substantial-evidence review. Justice Sotomayor’s uniformity concern is legitimate, yet the textual way to address it is de novo correction of genuine legal errors (wrong standard, impermissible categorical rule, ignored required factors), not relabeling a record-intensive application as “law” to evade Congress’s compelled-evidence constraint. On this scheme, once the agency applies the correct persecution standard, courts may not reweigh the harm’s severity on a cold record absent evidence that compels the opposite conclusion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan offer the strongest reconciliation—de novo only for misstated standards, categorical rules, or ignored factors, and otherwise substantial-evidence review under § 1252(b)(4)(B)—and I take seriously their administrability concern and reliance on Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai. But that approach still risks reclassifying the ultimate application of the statutory term “persecution” as an “administrative finding of fact,” allowing § 1252(b)(4)(B) to swallow § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s preservation of “questions of law” as construed in Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, particularly where the underlying events are undisputed or agency-found. Nasrallah reinforces deference for factual challenges, yet it does not require treating the legal characterization step as effectively unreviewable; we can cabin de novo review to the legal calibration of the persecution threshold while remaining fully deferential on credibility, historical facts, and contested inferences. Given the stakes for vulnerable applicants and the need for doctrinal consistency in a recurring statutory standard, I would retain de novo review for whether settled facts meet the legal definition of persecution.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right to press Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson: some mixed questions count as “questions of law” under § 1252(a)(2)(D), and courts must correct true legal misapplications. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, that preservation clause must be reconciled with § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s specific command that “administrative findings of fact” are conclusive unless the record compels the contrary; in our immigration practice (Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai), the persecution determination on a particular record has been treated as a severity-and-context judgment reviewed under that compelled-evidence/substantial-evidence framework. I agree with Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson that de novo review remains for misstatements of the persecution standard, ignored required considerations, or impermissible categorical rules; what I cannot accept is recharacterizing the agency’s record-bound calibration as de novo “law,” which would invite appellate reweighing and drain § 1252(b)(4)(B) of independent force. Under a pragmatic textualist reading, the workable middle ground is: de novo for genuine legal error, but deferential review for the agency’s application of the correct standard to this applicant’s facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing proposal seriously: de novo only for misstatements, categorical rules, or ignored factors, and otherwise substantial-evidence review under § 1252(b)(4)(B). But that reconciliation still assumes the dispositive “persecution” classification is itself an “administrative finding of fact,” when § 1252(a)(2)(D) (as read in Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson) preserves judicial review of at least some applications of legal standards to settled facts; otherwise Congress’s preservation of “questions of law” becomes vanishingly small in the very cases where it matters. Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai properly bar appellate reweighing of disputed historical facts and inferences, but they do not require us to treat a statutory threshold determination as insulated whenever the agency recites the right words—misapplication of the standard to found facts is a legal error courts remain competent (and obligated) to correct. Nasrallah reinforces deference for factual challenges, yet it does not authorize converting the legal characterization step Congress preserved into an effectively unreviewable “factfinding.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson treat some mixed questions as “questions of law” under § 1252(a)(2)(D), and Justice Sotomayor is right that we must not let deference swallow genuine legal-error review. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1252(b)(4)(B) is a specific, mandatory instruction that administrative factfinding is conclusive unless the record compels the opposite, and our immigration precedents (Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai in particular) have consistently treated the persecution line on a given record as a severity-and-context judgment reviewed for substantial evidence rather than de novo. I can accommodate Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson by preserving de novo review for true legal errors—misstating the persecution standard, using impermissible categorical rules, or ignoring required considerations—without recharacterizing routine application-to-facts as “law” in a way that would invite appellate reweighing and undermine the statute’s structure. Under an institutionalist, precedent- and text-focused approach, that reconciliation gives real effect to both § 1252(a)(2)(D) and § 1252(b)(4)(B) while maintaining administrable review in a high-volume docket.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson treat some applications of law to settled facts as “questions of law” preserved by § 1252(a)(2)(D), and Justice Sotomayor rightly worries about doctrinal uniformity if “persecution” line-drawing is insulated. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1252(b)(4)(B) is a more specific instruction about the conclusiveness of “administrative findings of fact” absent compulsion, and our immigration precedents (Elias-Zacarias, Ming Dai, and Nasrallah) repeatedly apply that “compels” framework to eligibility determinations that are dominated by severity, frequency, and context on a particular record. The sound textual reconciliation is to read § 1252(a)(2)(D) to preserve de novo review for genuine legal errors—misstating the persecution standard, adopting a categorical rule, or ignoring legally required considerations—while treating the agency’s record-bound application of the correct standard as reviewed under the compelled-evidence/substantial-evidence constraint. Under that approach, uniformity is pursued through correction of legal misstatements rather than appellate reweighing of degree on a cold record, which Congress appears to have foreclosed in § 1252(b)(4)(B).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed reconciliation—de novo review only for a misstated standard, ignored factors, or categorical rules—has real institutional appeal, but it still treats the agency’s ultimate “persecution” characterization as effectively factual so long as the agency recites the right words, which is exactly where under-calibrated thresholds can persist. Justice Kagan is right that Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai warn against appellate reweighing, yet those cases are best read as constraining review of historical facts and inferential factfinding (e.g., motive), not as converting the application of a statutory term to settled facts into an unreviewable “finding of fact” under § 1252(b)(4)(B). Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, confirm that Congress preserved review of at least some mixed questions as “questions of law” under § 1252(a)(2)(D), and I think the persecution-threshold calibration on undisputed facts fits there without undermining deference on credibility and what happened. Pragmatically and with an eye toward procedural fairness and consequences, that division gives meaningful judicial review where it matters most—when the facts are settled but the legal threshold may be applied too stingily—while still preventing routine relitigation of the record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress has directed that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), which embodies substantial-evidence review for fact-bound determinations in asylum cases. Under INS v. Elias-Zacarias, a court of appeals may not overturn the agency’s conclusion unless the record compels the opposite result; that framework fits naturally where the “persecution” inquiry turns on the severity, frequency, and context of harm and threats. Courts remain free to review de novo any legal error in articulating the persecution standard, but the application of that standard to a particular record is predominantly factual and should not be converted into more searching appellate review. A narrow holding preserving the INA’s review scheme and longstanding precedent best serves institutional legitimacy and uniformity in the administration of immigration law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review text directs that “the administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), which by its terms requires substantial-evidence review of the agency’s factual determinations in removal proceedings. Whether particular threats and mistreatment are sufficiently severe and persistent to constitute “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is an intensely fact-bound judgment entrusted to the IJ and BIA, and appellate courts may not reweigh the evidence under a more searching standard. This Court’s articulation of the “record compels” constraint in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), aligns with Congress’s choice to limit judicial second-guessing of agency factfinding in this context. Nothing in the statutory text authorizes de novo appellate substitution on persecution determinations, and fidelity to the enacted standard of review requires affirmance absent a compelled contrary conclusion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme directs courts to treat the agency’s factual determinations as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the question whether particular threats and mistreatment cross the line into “persecution” is, in this posture, a fact-intensive application that Congress meant to entrust primarily to the immigration factfinder. INS v. Elias-Zacarias confirms that core asylum-eligibility determinations are reviewed under the substantial-evidence/“record compels” standard, and petitioners’ argument largely asks appellate courts to reweigh severity, frequency, and context—precisely what deferential review forbids. Whatever the proper characterization of some mixed questions in other settings, a more searching appellate standard here would undermine Congress’s choice of deference in immigration adjudication and invite inconsistent second-guessing of agency line-drawing with significant practical consequences for enforcement and administrability. Accordingly, the court of appeals properly applied substantial-evidence review to the agency’s no-persecution determination.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Whether established threats and mistreatment rise to the statutory threshold of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is best understood as a mixed question of law and fact—an application of a legal standard to settled facts—so courts of appeals should not treat it as pure factfinding insulated by 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s substantial-evidence constraint. Under U.S. Bank N.A. v. Village at Lakeridge, de novo review is appropriate where the inquiry is primarily about applying and elaborating a legal standard in a way that provides guidance across cases, and “persecution” is precisely the kind of recurring, legally bounded concept that demands uniformity. INS v. Elias-Zacarias does not compel a different result because it applied substantial-evidence review to the agency’s factual determination about motive, not to the general, across-case calibration of what counts as “persecution.” More searching review here better protects access to justice for asylum seekers and mitigates inconsistency in a system where erroneous under-recognition of persecution can have life-or-death consequences for vulnerable applicants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s review provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs courts to treat “administrative findings of fact” as “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” which is the substantial-evidence standard. This Court has repeatedly applied that framework to asylum-eligibility determinations, including whether an applicant “was persecuted in the past or fears persecution in the future,” describing those as fact questions reviewed deferentially. See INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992); Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357, 362, 365 (2021); Nasrallah v. Barr, 590 U.S. 573, 584 (2020). While courts retain de novo authority to correct legal misstatements of the persecution standard, the agency’s fact-bound application of that standard to a particular record is reviewable only for substantial evidence, which best fits Congress’s text and promotes administrable, coherent judicial review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA distinguishes between deferential review of agency “findings of fact,” which are conclusive unless “any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and judicial resolution of “questions of law,” § 1252(a)(2)(D). Whether established threats and mistreatment satisfy the statutory standard of “persecution” in § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a mixed question—application of a legal standard to settled facts—and this Court has held such mixed questions are reviewable as “questions of law.” Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 589 U.S. 221, 227–28 (2020); see also Wilkinson v. Garland, 601 U.S. 209, 218–21 (2024). Congress’s choice to specify substantial-evidence deference for factfinding, while preserving judicial review for legal questions, counsels against extending highly deferential review to the legal threshold of “persecution.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme directs courts to treat the agency’s determinations as conclusive unless “any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the question whether particular threats and mistreatment rise to the level of “persecution” is a highly fact-dependent application that Congress has placed within that deferential framework. INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), applied the “record compels” formulation in reviewing the agency’s determination on an asylum-eligibility element, reflecting this Court’s longstanding practice of substantial-evidence review for the agency’s evaluation of severity, context, and credibility in asylum cases. While petitioners invoke mixed-question cases such as U.S. Bank to argue for more searching review, the more workable and institutionally modest approach is to preserve substantial-evidence review here, reserving de novo review for genuine legal errors about the definition of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A). Maintaining the established standard promotes uniformity and administrability across the immigration docket and respects the agency’s factfinding role as Congress contemplated.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s review rule directs that “the administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), a highly deferential standard that naturally covers the agency’s determination—on a particular record—whether alleged threats and mistreatment are severe enough to constitute “persecution” under § 1101(a)(42)(A). In INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), we applied the “compels” formulation to an asylum-eligibility determination involving application of statutory terms to evidence, reinforcing Congress’s choice to cabin appellate reweighing of fact-bound judgments. While U.S. Bank’s mixed-question framework can require de novo review when the issue is primarily legal, persecution determinations typically hinge on the intensity, frequency, and context of harm—matters better characterized as factfinding within § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s domain. More searching review risks displacing the agency’s role and upsetting the methodology Congress prescribed for judicial review in immigration cases.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s substantial-evidence rule, codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), properly governs agency factfinding, but whether undisputed threats and mistreatment satisfy the statutory “persecution” element in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a mixed question involving the application of a legal standard to established facts. Consistent with U.S. Bank’s instruction that applying settled legal principles is “legal work” warranting de novo review, courts of appeals should not treat the persecution threshold as an unreviewable, fact-bound call when the agency’s decision turns on the meaning and uniform application of that legal standard. INS v. Elias-Zacarias confirms deference to fact determinations and the “record compels” formulation for reversing agency findings, but it should not be read to require substantial-evidence review of the legal characterization of established facts as (non-)persecution. More searching review here promotes procedural fairness and uniformity in asylum adjudication without displacing Congress’s deference to the agency on genuine historical fact disputes.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review under the deferential substantial-evidence standard the agency’s determination that the petitioner’s alleged threats and physical mistreatment do not amount to “persecution” for asylum purposes, or instead treat that determination as a legal question warranting less deferential review.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the concept of “persecution”); related judicial-review framework in the INA requiring substantial-evidence review for administrative factual findings in removal/asylum cases (commonly applied under 8 U.S.C. § 1252).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that whether proven harms (e.g., threats plus physical mistreatment) rise to the legal level of “persecution” is not a purely factual finding entitled to substantial-evidence deference; rather, it is at least a mixed question—often treated as a legal determination or application-of-law-to-fact—that should receive more searching appellate review to promote consistency and correct legal standards in asylum adjudication.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues that the First Circuit correctly applied substantial-evidence review because the agency’s ‘no persecution’ determination is a fact-bound application of settled law to the particular record; Congress’s INA review scheme requires deference to the agency’s assessment of the severity and character of harm, and petitioners’ challenge amounts to disagreement with the agency’s factual evaluation rather than identification of any legal error.
key_precedents: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024) (cited by respondent in framing the case as fact-bound rather than a pure legal question)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that labeling the persecution determination as “factual” could let the agency ratchet the threshold downward and defeat uniformity—highlights a real institutional concern, but it does not overcome Congress’s specific instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative findings of fact are conclusive absent compulsion. The minimalist way through is to preserve de novo correction for genuine legal error, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett emphasize (categorical misdefinition of “persecution,” or a rule that certain harms can never qualify), while treating the run-of-the-mill severity line-drawing on a particular record as a substantial-evidence question. Guerrero-Lasprilla, as Justice Gorsuch notes, spoke to jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D) and expressly did not set a standard of review, so it cannot displace § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s separate, controlling review command. On that understanding, we can maintain uniform statutory meaning where it matters without inviting appellate reweighing of degree and context in individual cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that mislabeling the persecution determination as “fact” could allow the agency to ratchet the legal baseline and frustrate uniformity, but that concern is answered by keeping de novo review for genuine definitional or categorical legal error about what “persecution” means under § 1101(a)(42)(A). Where, as Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the agency applies a settled legal standard to a record-specific severity assessment, § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s text makes those fact-bound determinations conclusive unless the record compels the contrary; courts may not reweigh degree-and-context line-drawing by redescribing it as “law.” Guerrero-Lasprilla, as Justice Gorsuch notes, was a jurisdictional restoration case under § 1252(a)(2)(D) and expressly did not set a standard of review, so it cannot displace Congress’s separate substantial-evidence command in § 1252(b)(4)(B). Elias-Zacarias confirms that, absent a compelled contrary conclusion or a misstatement of the governing standard, appellate courts must respect agency primacy in these heavily fact-dependent eligibility applications.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the uniformity concern—that labeling the persecution determination as “fact” could let the agency quietly narrow the statutory baseline. But under the text Congress wrote, § 1252(b)(4)(B) makes “administrative findings of fact” conclusive unless the record compels the opposite, and the persecution call in the ordinary case is predominantly a degree-and-context judgment about the gravity of harms on a particular record, not an abstract articulation of the statutory meaning. As Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, we can preserve de novo correction for genuine legal error—where the agency adopts a categorical misdefinition or rule—without converting close, record-bound severity line-drawing into appellate reweighing forbidden by § 1252(b)(4)(B). Guerrero-Lasprilla, as Justice Gorsuch notes, addressed jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D) and expressly did not set a standard of review, so it cannot displace Congress’s separate substantial-evidence directive; Loper Bright likewise reinforces our duty to decide meaning when meaning is disputed, not to redo fact-intensive applications when it is not.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justices Thomas/Alito’s strongest point is that § 1252(b)(4)(B) reflects Congress’s choice to bar appellate reweighing of record-specific degree judgments, and I agree we must treat credibility, historical facts, and subsidiary severity findings as conclusive absent compulsion. But that argument assumes the classification question: as Justice Kagan emphasizes, whether established harms meet the statutory threshold of “persecution” is an application of law to fact, and reading “findings of fact” to swallow that inquiry risks letting the agency effectively recalibrate the legal baseline case by case while insulating nonuniformity. Justice Gorsuch is right that Guerrero-Lasprilla is jurisdictional and does not itself dictate de novo review, yet it underscores that mixed applications can be “legal” in character—so we must police the boundary of § 1252(b)(4)(B) rather than letting its substantial-evidence command attach by label. After Loper Bright, I am especially unwilling to permit functional narrowing of § 1101(a)(42)(A) through deference masquerading as factfinding when the real-world consequence is to deny protection to vulnerable applicants based on an unreviewable, shifting severity threshold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that § 1252(b)(4)(B) cabins courts to substantial-evidence review and guards against appellate reweighing of severity, but that textual command extends only to “administrative findings of fact,” not to the legal characterization of those facts against a statutory threshold. Justice Gorsuch is right that Guerrero-Lasprilla’s mixed-question language was jurisdictional and did not itself supply a standard of review, yet that simply returns us to the antecedent classification question—what is properly a “finding of fact” under § 1252(b)(4)(B)—and I do not think the statute or Elias-Zacarias compels treating the ultimate persecution determination as purely factual when the underlying events and their gravity are conceded. After Loper Bright, courts have a heightened obligation to supply a uniform meaning for “persecution” in § 1101(a)(42)(A), and meaningful review of whether established facts meet that legal threshold is necessary to prevent de facto baseline drift while still deferring to historical facts, credibility, and subsidiary severity findings. Roberts’s proposed safety valve—de novo only for “categorical misdefinition”—is too thin, because the operative legal line can be narrowed through repeated case-specific characterizations insulated as “fact.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson persuasively caution that calling the persecution determination “factual” could let a legally cramped baseline hide inside fact-labeling and erode uniformity, and after Loper Bright we must independently correct any misdefinition of the statutory term. But the textual command Congress wrote in § 1252(b)(4)(B)—that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive” unless the record compels the contrary—still governs when the agency applies an accepted legal definition to a record-specific severity-and-context judgment; reclassifying that application as “law” risks inviting precisely the forbidden appellate reweighing. As the Chief Justice stresses, Guerrero-Lasprilla addressed what counts as a “question of law” for jurisdictional restoration under § 1252(a)(2)(D) and expressly did not set a standard of review, so it cannot displace § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s separate review directive. The best reconciliation is to preserve de novo correction for genuine categorical or definitional legal errors about “persecution,” while otherwise applying substantial-evidence review to this predominantly fact-bound threshold-crossing determination, consistent with our practice in Elias-Zacarias.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that treating the persecution determination as “factual” could mask a de facto legal narrowing and erode national uniformity after Loper Bright. But that concern is adequately handled by preserving de novo correction for genuine legal misdefinitions or categorical rules, while still honoring Congress’s specific instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative factfinding is conclusive absent a record that compels the contrary. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Guerrero-Lasprilla’s mixed-question language was jurisdictional and expressly did not set the standard of review, so it cannot displace § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s substantial-evidence regime for this record-bound severity line-drawing. Elias-Zacarias and longstanding asylum-review practice confirm that, absent identified legal error, courts should not relabel degree-and-context judgments as “law” in order to reweigh the evidence.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor raise the most serious concern: if we treat the ultimate “persecution” determination as a mere factfinding, the agency could effectively narrow the statutory baseline without meaningful appellate correction, impairing uniformity. But under the INA’s text, § 1252(b)(4)(B) makes “administrative findings of fact” conclusive absent a compelled contrary conclusion, and in this case the agency did not announce a categorical or definitional rule about what “persecution” means—it engaged in record-specific severity line-drawing. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Guerrero-Lasprilla’s mixed-question language was jurisdictional and expressly did not displace Congress’s separate standard-of-review command, so it cannot be used to reclassify this factbound application to permit de novo reweighing. Loper Bright reinforces that we must independently fix the meaning of “persecution” when the agency misstates it, but it does not authorize appellate courts to second-guess close, context-dependent severity judgments where the legal standard is undisputed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is textual—§ 1252(b)(4)(B) makes “administrative findings of fact” conclusive absent compulsion—and I agree it bars courts from redoing credibility, historical facts, and subsidiary severity determinations on a cold record. But that provision cannot resolve the antecedent classification question by ipse dixit: whether the ultimate “persecution” determination is itself a “finding of fact” or an application of a statutory threshold to settled facts, and I remain persuaded (with Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor) that treating the threshold-crossing decision as purely factual lets the agency effectively recalibrate the legal baseline case-by-case while insulating nonuniformity. Justice Gorsuch is right that Guerrero-Lasprilla was jurisdictional and did not itself announce a de novo standard of review, yet it reinforces that applying statutory language to established facts can be a legal question—leaving § 1252(b)(4)(B) to do its proper work on what happened, not to foreclose meaningful judicial oversight of the statutory line. Elias-Zacarias, as Justice Roberts invokes it, involved motive and inference under substantial-evidence review and does not compel collapsing the statutory “persecution” threshold into unreviewable factfinding when the dispute is about the legal characterization of conceded harms rather than what occurred.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress directed that "administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary," 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s assessment whether particular threats and mistreatment are sufficiently severe to constitute “persecution” is a record-driven, fact-intensive judgment. Our cases have long applied substantial-evidence review to core asylum-eligibility determinations, including analogous applications of statutory standards to particular facts, see INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), and I would avoid recharacterizing that settled practice in a way that invites broad relitigation of asylum outcomes in the courts of appeals. A narrow ruling for the government preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to the INA’s review framework and leaving room for de novo correction only where the agency applies an incorrect legal definition of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A). Petitioners’ disagreement here sounds chiefly in the agency’s evaluation of severity and context, which is precisely what substantial-evidence review is meant to respect.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and Congress repeatedly frames asylum eligibility determinations as matters for the “trier of fact,” including whether an applicant has established persecution. In INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), this Court applied substantial-evidence review to asylum-eligibility determinations, confirming that courts may not reweigh the record or substitute their judgment for the agency’s absent compulsion to the contrary. Whether particular threats and mistreatment, on this record, rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-bound application of an established statutory term in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A), fitting comfortably within the substantial-evidence regime Congress prescribed. Treating that determination as de novo “legal” review would dilute § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s text and expand judicial power beyond what the statute permits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s determination that particular threats and mistreatment do not rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-bound application of that settled standard to a specific record. This Court has repeatedly described asylum-eligibility determinations as reviewed for substantial evidence, and in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), we emphasized that a court of appeals may not reverse unless the evidence compels the opposite conclusion. Petitioners’ approach would invite de novo appellate reweighing of severity and credibility assessments that Congress assigned to immigration judges and the BIA, undermining the practical efficiency and finality that § 1252 embodies. Absent a showing that the agency applied the wrong legal standard, the court of appeals must apply substantial-evidence review to the “no persecution” finding.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Although 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) requires substantial-evidence deference to the agency’s underlying factual findings, whether established harms meet the statutory threshold of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is best understood as an application-of-law-to-fact question requiring meaningful appellate oversight to ensure uniform, fair standards. Treating “persecution” as purely factual risks insulating inconsistent or unduly cramped interpretations that can disproportionately deny protection to vulnerable asylum seekers facing serious threats and mistreatment. The older circuit cases often describe eligibility as “factual,” but that does not eliminate the judiciary’s duty to correct legal mischaracterizations of the severity and legal significance of proven harm, especially where the agency’s reasoning effectively sets a categorical rule. Nothing in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), compels converting this quintessential legal-threshold inquiry into an unreviewable fact determination; it instead underscores courts’ responsibility to say what the law is.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s review provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), clearly commands substantial-evidence review for “administrative findings of fact,” but whether established facts (threats plus physical mistreatment) satisfy the statutory term “persecution” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is best understood as an application-of-law-to-fact question that requires meaningful appellate supervision to ensure consistent legal thresholds. INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), applied substantial-evidence review to the agency’s predictive and motive-related factual determinations and does not definitively resolve the standard for this kind of mixed question; treating its single sentence about “eligibility” as controlling would read too much into a context-specific decision. A less deferential standard for the persecution determination (while still deferring on underlying historical facts and credibility) better fits statutory coherence and workability by reducing circuit-to-circuit and case-to-case variability in what counts as “persecution” without inviting de novo reweighing of evidence. After Loper Bright, courts must independently determine the best reading of statutory terms, and that supports more searching review of the agency’s legal characterization of proven harm even within the INA’s generally deferential scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s review rule directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s assessment whether particular threats and mistreatment are sufficiently severe to qualify as “persecution” is a case-specific application of a settled legal standard to a record—i.e., a predominantly factual determination warranting substantial-evidence review. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr and Wilkinson v. Garland construed § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s jurisdictional phrase “questions of law” to include mixed questions, but both expressly separated that jurisdictional inquiry from the standard-of-review question and thus do not displace § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s text. Respecting Congress’s allocation of decisionmaking authority in the removal system and our traditional deference to agency factfinding, a court of appeals may correct genuine legal error about the meaning of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A), but it should not reweigh the severity of harms absent a record that compels the contrary conclusion. That approach preserves separation of powers without reviving broad agency deference on legal meaning.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the INA’s judicial-review scheme, courts of appeals must uphold the agency’s determinations if supported by substantial evidence, see 8 U.S.C. § 1252, and the assessment whether particular threats and mistreatment are sufficiently severe to constitute “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a highly fact-bound application of a settled standard. Consistent with our approach in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), appellate courts do not reweigh the record but ask whether a reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to reach the opposite conclusion. Treating “persecution” categorizations as broadly de novo legal questions would risk undermining workability and the intended deference to the agency’s front-line judgment in individualized asylum cases. Absent a showing that the agency applied the wrong legal standard, substantial-evidence review is the proper lens for this determination.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s assessment that the specific threats and mistreatment in this record do not rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-intensive application of a settled statutory standard rather than a freestanding legal interpretation. Consistent with INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), courts of appeals may not reweigh the severity and character of harms and must uphold the agency so long as substantial evidence supports its conclusion. While mixed questions can sometimes warrant less deferential review, nothing in § 1101(a)(42)(A)’s text or § 1252’s review framework suggests Congress intended de novo appellate substitution on this kind of case-specific persecution determination, particularly absent an identified legal error in the governing standard. Precedent and methodological consistency therefore counsel substantial-evidence review here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s substantial-evidence rule in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) properly governs the agency’s historical factfinding (what happened, how often, and with what severity), but whether those established facts meet the statutory concept of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is at least a mixed question requiring meaningful appellate supervision to ensure consistent legal standards. Treating “persecution” as purely factual risks insulating from review legal line-drawing that has profound practical consequences for asylum seekers and invites uneven adjudication across circuits and IJs, undermining procedural fairness. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr confirms that “questions of law” in the INA encompass mixed questions of applying law to fact, and while it disclaimed deciding a standard-of-review issue, its reasoning supports recognizing the legal character of the persecution determination so courts can correct misapplications of the governing standard. A less deferential approach to the legal component still respects agency factfinding while ensuring that the statutory threshold for “persecution” is not effectively rewritten through unduly deferential review.
